item.title: Quantum optimization beyond qubit count by low-energy subspace sampling
item.description:
Skim new method — Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent reaches an approximation ratio above 0.95 on a 10000-variable HUBO instance using 100 circuit executions on up to 152 qubits of an IBM processor.

Grade 0.443 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm: Performance, Mechanism, and Impleme…”

Figure

Approximation ratio versus algorithm iterations for a 10000-variable heavy-hex HUBO instance on IBM hardware and classical simulation, showing convergence above 0.95 within 100 iterations.

Asks

How can quantum optimization algorithms be scaled to practical problem sizes far exceeding available qubit counts without losing the problem's global structure?

Before

Hardware demonstrations of standard quantum optimization algorithms remained limited to a few hundred variables, or required variational optimization and amplitude estimation.

But

Still fails to match the solution quality of simulated annealing; subproblems can lose hardware-native bipartition when non-adjacent variables are frozen; evaluated on at most 10000 variables and 152 physical qubits.

Tools

Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD) · fixed-angle QAOA sampler · IBM Heron and Nighthawk processors · bitflip local search

Abstract

On current digital quantum devices, standard one-qubit-per-variable encodings restrict quantum optimization algorithms to problem sizes where classical solvers typically excel. To avoid this constraint, we introduce Quantum Subspace Sampling Descent (QSSD), an iterative heuristic that decouples the number of problem variables from qubit count, while preserving knowledge of the problem's global structure. QSSD drives the energy descent using a fixed-angle Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm as a low-energy sampler. As the angles are precomputed, each iteration requires just a single circuit execution. We test QSSD on IBM Heron and Nighthawk quantum devices with up to 152 qubits on instances of higher-order unconstrained binary optimization and Max-cut problems. On the largest instance with 10000 variables, QSSD reaches an approximation ratio above 0.95 with 100 circuit executions. We provide both exact and heuristic classical baselines, namely greedy, branch-and-bound solver, and simulated annealing. While our approach still does not match the performance of the best classical baseline, it shows promise in a slower runtime scaling with problem size given a fixed budget. This suggests a regime of large problems where subspace sampling on quantum devices could become competitive, as we also demonstrate how improvements in hardware will lead to better algorithm performance. QSSD is thus a practical heuristic for combinatorial optimization problems that helps bring quantum optimization a step closer to utility.

item.arxave:action: Run the fixed-angle QAOA subspace sampler on the 16-qubit spin device for small MaxCut/HUBO instances and compare approximation ratio, circuit executions, CZ count, and depth against the IBM results.

item.arxave:action: Implement the QSSD loop and fixed-angle QAOA sampler as an optional MaxCut benchmark in the HPC-integrated stack, logging qubit count, two-qubit gate count, depth, and approximation ratio.
